What happens when 50 concurrent users attempt to book the exact same VIP shuttle seat at the exact same millisecond?
Double-booking? Frozen UI? Or a silent data race?
Most reservation systems look great in staging, but crumble under high-concurrency race conditions during peak flash sales.
In my latest architectural prototype, TransFlow AI — an executive intercity shuttle reservation platform for the Bandung – Jakarta corridor — I explored a resilient, production-grade architecture leveraging Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Optimistic UI rollback mechanisms, and action-oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
1️⃣ Optimistic UI with Instant Conflict Rollback:
Delivers instant 0ms perceived latency for passengers selecting seats. If a backend collision occurs (HTTP 409 Conflict), the UI immediately rolls back to its previous snapshot and gracefully marks the contested seat as held by another session—without breaking the user flow.
2️⃣ Anti-Race Distributed Atomic Lock:
Guarantees zero double-booking risk by securing seats through atomic locks with a 600-second (10-minute) TTL. Built-in stress test simulator executes 50 parallel bot threads competing for high-demand seats in real-time.
3️⃣ Action-Oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
The AI Concierge isn’t just a passive conversational bot. Through MCP tools, it acts as an autonomous operational copilot:
• Queries real-time tollway sensors (`get_corridor_telemetry`) to monitor weather radar and traffic bottlenecks along the Cipularang expressway.
• Dynamically calculates estimated arrival times (`calculate_dynamic_eta`).
• Grounded RAG with real physical constraints: The Toyota HiAce Premio stands at 2.28m, strictly barring it from entering the elevated MBZ tollway (2.10m clearance gantry)—enforcing routing through the lower expressway for structural safety.
4️⃣ Authentic Top-Down Automotive Blueprint:
A precision cabin blueprint reflecting Indonesian automotive ergonomics: Right-Hand Drive (RHD) cockpit, curbside electric sliding door, and a distinct separation between 100% Flat Floor seats (Rows 1 & 2) vs. Rear Wheel Well arch protrusions (Row 3).
🛠️ Tech Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript, Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Tailwind CSS, Model Context Protocol (MCP), Vector RAG, and jsPDF.

Over the past few months I've been building VenHub (Vendor Hub), an operations portal for vendors and internal teams at iForte Solusi Infotek. Field surveys and FTTH preventive maintenance used to run through many manual steps across several systems. VenHub moves that flow into one portal connected directly to Salesforce.

What VenHub does today: 
1. Connectivity Survey Salesforce sends surveys to vendors. Vendors fill in the Survey Form section by section, with photos per group. After submission, Salesforce creates or updates the Work Report and sends the status (Submitted, Approved or Rejected) back to VenHub.
2. Automatic PHS documents When a survey is Approved, the system calculates quantities against the PHS price list, generates the PDF, and uploads it to the Work Report in Salesforce. Failed deliveries retry automatically and can also be resent manually.
3. FTTH Preventive Maintenance Technicians submit a Customer ID, a category, and evidence photos. The photo count is validated against the category. Salesforce then sends the Work Order and Service Appointment status back.

What's next We plan to move more of the FTTH business process into VenHub, so vendors and internal teams work from one place.

Security and personal data protection VenHub holds customer and vendor data, so I built this in from the start, using Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP) as the reference:
1. Email OTP login, plus mandatory Microsoft Authenticator for Super Admins and Admins
2. Temporary account lock after repeated failed logins, and automatic logout when idle
3. Personal data masked in logs and in views for roles that shouldn't see it
4. Access to personal data recorded: who, which role, which endpoint
5. Automatic data retention for logs, histories and notifications

Tech stack:
1. Backend: Go (Gin), PostgreSQL, JWT, TOTP
2. Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, Zustand, React Hook Form + Zod, acting as a BFF so the browser never handles the API token
3. Integrations: Salesforce (Apex/LWC and REST), internal email service
4. Deployment: Docker & Jenkins

What I learned:
1. Two-way integration needs retries, idempotency, and clear logs, or small failures are hard to trace.
2. Security and privacy cost far less when built in from the beginning.
3. As developers, we have to solve problems, keep learning, and adapt to whatever comes up. We shouldn't idolize a single platform, because a developer needs to see the big picture and pick the tools that will actually help the company.

A QA/QC report should do more than record what happened yesterday.

It should help the project team understand what needs attention today.

On a busy project, there can be hundreds of inspections, defects, approvals, corrective actions and open items moving at the same time.

If that information is only discussed at a weekly meeting, some issues may already have moved downstream before the right people see them.

• What was inspected
• What passed
• What failed
• What remains open
• What corrective action is required
• Who owns the next action
• What could affect upcoming work
• Which issues are beginning to repeat

That last point matters.

One isolated issue may be manageable.

The same issue appearing across three areas may be telling you something much more important.

Good reporting helps turn site observations into early warning information.

Captive Power, Microgrids & Clean Energy Integration in West Java Industrial Estates: Enhancing Data Center Resilience in Cikarang & Karawang

As hyperscale and enterprise data centers expand across West Java’s industrial belt—spanning Cikarang, Karawang, and Purwakarta—reliable electricity remains the defining foundation of digital infrastructure bankability. 

While the regional high-voltage grid provides essential backbone power, rising load concentration and global tenant decarbonization mandates are driving developers to evaluate industrial estate microgrids, behind-the-meter renewables, and clean backup architectures.

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, integrated power solutions in West Java achieve institutional bankability only when grid-parallel synchronization, regulatory compliance, and 24/7 reliability are engineered upfront.

Treating captive clean power or microgrids as ad-hoc add-ons creates synchronization risks, regulatory friction, and stranded CAPEX.

Six core pillars define bankable captive power and microgrid integration for West Java data centers:

 1. Grid-Parallel Synchronization & Protection Engineering: Integrating on-site solar, gas/biofuel firming, or battery storage alongside utility feeds requires precision protection relays, seamless islanding/re-synchronization, and strict power-quality stability.

 2. Industrial Estate Power-Supply & Regulatory Compliance: Bankable architectures align strictly with Indonesia’s electricity supply rules, industrial-estate utility frameworks, and parallel-operation charges to avoid retroactive regulatory exposure.

 3. BESS Firming & Clean Backup Transition:  Replacing or supplementing conventional diesel backup with Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) or sustainable biofuels reduces emissions while supporting peak shaving and transient ride-through.

 4. 24/7 Clean Energy Matching & Auditable Scope 2 Integrity: Combining behind-the-meter solar, utility clean tariffs, and accredited Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) gives global cloud tenants verifiable low-carbon power attribution.

 5. Phased Capacity Scaling & Balanced Offtake Terms: Because data center IT loads ramp across multi-year tenant fit-outs, captive power and storage investments must follow modular CAPEX stages tied to realistic load milestones.

 6. Tier-One EPC, Fire/HSE Safety & ABAC Governance: Institutional lenders require proven mission-critical EPC execution, stringent battery/fuel fire-suppression compliance, and strict anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) controls.

The Future of SAP Development: How AI and Automation Are Transforming Enterprise Systems 🚀💻
Enterprise technology is evolving rapidly, and SAP continues to play an important role in helping organizations manage complex business operations.
As businesses accelerate their digital transformation, SAP development is moving beyond traditional customization toward more intelligent, integrated, and automated enterprise solutions.
I believe three key trends will shape the future of SAP development:
🔹 AI-Powered Enterprise Applications
Artificial Intelligence is creating new opportunities to automate business processes, improve data analysis, and support faster decision-making. Integrating AI capabilities into enterprise systems can help organizations operate more efficiently.
🔹 Modern ABAP Development & Clean Core
Modern SAP development increasingly emphasizes maintainable code, reusable components, and upgrade-friendly extensions. Developers need to balance business-specific requirements with long-term system stability and scalability.
🔹 Enterprise Integration & Process Automation

🌏 Throwback to Carbon Forward Asia 2026. Conversations, Connections and Insights Shaping the Future of Carbon Markets.

Looking back at my experience at Carbon Forward Asia 2026, held on 24–25 March in Singapore, it was an incredibly valuable opportunity to engage with policymakers, carbon-market professionals, project developers, standard-setting organizations and industry leaders from across the global carbon ecosystem.

What made this event particularly worthwhile was the breadth of discussions. From international carbon-market mechanisms and compliance frameworks to carbon removals, nature-based solutions and emerging methodologies, the conference offered a comprehensive perspective on where the industry is heading.

Here are some of the discussions, interactions and takeaways that stood out.

1. Article 6 and the evolution of international carbon markets

Several discussions explored the implementation of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, particularly the development of bilateral agreements, corresponding adjustments, host-country authorisations and the Article 6.4 mechanism.

An interesting area was the geopolitical dimension of international carbon-credit transactions, including the importance of partner-country selection, governance structures, MRV capacity and alignment with the Paris Agreement.

The discussions also raised important questions about the availability of eligible credits, quality requirements, additional safeguards and the ability of countries to scale credible supply.

2. CBAM: The growing intersection between carbon pricing and international trade

The sessions examining the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) were particularly insightful.

Discussions covered the potential cost implications for Asian exporters, the expansion of compliance requirements and the implications for industrial competitiveness.

Presentations examining carbon-pricing developments across China, South Korea, Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam and Malaysia highlighted how domestic carbon-pricing mechanisms are becoming increasingly relevant to international trade.

The discussions involving Louis Kay (CFO, Meranti Green Steel) andDanielle King (Director, RESET Carbon Ltd. 锐思碳管理) also provided an industry perspective on the real costs and implications of CBAM.

One key takeaway was that developing credible domestic carbon-pricing and emissions-reporting systems will be increasingly important for Asian economies seeking to remain competitive in international markets.

3. CORSIA: Opportunities and challenges in aviation

I attended discussions on the adoption, implementation and limitations of the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).

The conversations explored eligible carbon credits, supply availability, insurance, compliance requirements, market liquidity and the challenges of translating regulatory demand into actual procurement.

It was particularly interesting to follow the perspectives of David Kitt, Chief Technology Officer at DelAgua Group, who participated in the CORSIA panel alongside representatives from Climate Impact X, Verra andMalaysia Aviation Group.

The discussion highlighted an important market challenge: developing eligible credit supply is only one part of the equation. Stronger procurement commitments, transparent pricing and accessible market infrastructure are equally important to building a functioning compliance market.

4. Carbon removals and nature-based solutions across APAC

Another particularly interesting session was Removals and Their Role in Net Zero – Regional APAC Initiatives and Case Studies.

The panel brought together perspectives from conservation, financial institutions, carbon-removal technologies and project development.

It included Kash Burnett, Global Head of Carbon Removal Technologies at HSBC, Matteo Marinelli of WWF, and Rob Raffael Kardinal, Chairman of the Indonesia Carbon Credit and Biodiversity Alliance and Co-founder of the SERCOVA project.

The discussions explored the role of nature-based removals, emerging carbon-removal technologies, financing opportunities and the practical challenges of scaling projects across the region.

The SERCOVA example was particularly relevant in understanding how forest conservation and improved forest management initiatives can contribute to climate mitigation while supporting biodiversity and sustainable development.

5. Carbon-credit methodologies, standards and integrity

One of the most valuable parts of my visit was the opportunity to connect with representatives from Verra and exchange perspectives on existing and forthcoming carbon-credit methodologies.

We discussed the continued evolution of methodologies, project requirements and the importance of robust standards in maintaining the credibility of carbon projects.

I also valued the opportunity to connect withDuncan van Bergen, Co-founder of Calyx Global, whose organisation works on independent carbon-credit ratings and assessments of credit quality.

These conversations reinforced the importance of looking beyond credit volumes and understanding the underlying environmental integrity, additionality, permanence and impact of individual projects.

6. Conversations with policymakers and international stakeholders

Beyond the formal conference sessions, one of the most memorable aspects was the opportunity to engage with policymakers.

I had the opportunity to meet with the Honourable Deputy Minister of Natural Resources, Government of Malawi, to discuss Malawi’s carbon-market roadmap and its ambitions for developing its national carbon-market ecosystem.

The exchange offered an interesting opportunity to discuss the development of national carbon-market frameworks, institutional readiness and the opportunities for countries to participate in international carbon markets.

I also had the opportunity to connect with professionals from organisations including Munich Re, DelAgua Group, Calyx Global, Verra and other participants across the carbon-market value chain.

These interactions provided valuable perspectives on the different roles that policy, project development, insurance, ratings, standards and investment play in building a functioning carbon-market ecosystem.

⸻

My broader takeaway from Carbon Forward Asia 2026

The carbon-market landscape is evolving beyond a relatively standalone voluntary market.

We are increasingly seeing the intersection of:

• International mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

• Compliance-driven demand through CORSIA and emerging regulatory frameworks.

• Carbon-pricing mechanisms and their implications for international trade through CBAM.

• Growing scrutiny of carbon-credit quality, methodologies and environmental integrity.

• Greater attention towards nature-based solutions, carbon removals and project financing.

• Increasing involvement of governments, financial institutions and corporates in developing and participating in carbon markets.

For Asia, this presents significant opportunities, but also substantial challenges around regulatory readiness, project quality, market infrastructure, financing and international alignment.

This sits well with the context of India’s rollout of the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency. There still remain concerns with the compatibility of hard-to-abate sectors to EU’s CBAM, the solution to which can drive significant tailwinds to India’s carbon markets.

My biggest reflection is that the next phase of carbon-market development will be defined not simply by how many credits we can generate, but by how effectively we can build credible markets that deliver measurable climate outcomes.

Grateful for the insightful discussions, professional connections and the opportunity to exchange perspectives with people working across different parts of this evolving industry.

A worthwhile experience, and certainly one that left me with plenty to think about as the global carbon-market landscape continues to develop.

🌱 The future of carbon markets will depend on the intersection of policy, integrity, finance and real-world climate impact.

Understanding Long-Term Dynamics in the Abadi Masela Gas Project Ecosystem: Aligning Patience, Governance, and Supporting Infrastructure Bankability

Mega-scale liquefied natural gas (LNG) developments—exemplified by Indonesia’s strategic Abadi Masela gas ecosystem in Eastern Indonesia—operate on multi-decade horizons that differ fundamentally from standard commercial infrastructure. 

Between upstream Front-End Engineering Design (FEED), Final Investment Decision (FID), marine terminal construction, and downstream industrial off-take, supporting infrastructure developers must navigate extended development cycles. 

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, third-party logistics, port, utility, and industrial support projects around Masela reach financial close only when capital patience, schedule synchronization, and tier-one compliance standards are engineered upfront.

Attempting to force short-term commercial timelines onto a mega-project ecosystem creates stranded capital and governance friction.

Six core pillars define bankable ecosystem participation around the Abadi Masela gas development:

 1. Multi-Year Horizon & Capital Patience Alignment: Institutional sponsors must structure equity and development capital to absorb multi-year upstream engineering milestones rather than relying on premature short-term cash flows.

 2. Schedule Synchronization With Upstream & Midstream Milestones:.Supporting jetties, laydown yards, workforce accommodations, and utility facilities must phase CAPEX deployment in lockstep with verified EPC mobilization schedules.

 3. Strict Compliance With International Operator Procurement Standards: Major upstream joint ventures enforce rigorous vendor pre-qualification across technical capacity, financial solvency, and local content (TKDN) verification.

 4. Remote Eastern Indonesia Marine & Civil Readiness: Delivering coastal infrastructure in Tanimbar and surrounding corridors requires early bathymetric surveys, cyclone/monsoon engineering, and self-reliant supply-chain logistics.

 5. Dual-Use Commercial Viability Beyond Construction Peaks: Bankable supporting assets—such as multi-purpose ports, water treatment, and clean power microgrids—are structured to serve long-term regional maritime and industrial demand beyond initial construction peaks.

 6. Zero-Tolerance ABAC, HSE & Indigenous Community Governance: Uncompromising anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) controls, international Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) systems, and transparent customary-land (*hak ulayat*) engagement are non-negotiable for institutional financiers.

PENETRANT TESTING: REVEALING SURFACE-BREAKING DEFECTS

Penetrant Testing (PT), is a widely used method for detecting surface-breaking discontinuities in non-porous materials.

The technique works based on the principle of capillary action, allowing liquid penetrant to enter small openings such as cracks, laps, seams, and surface-connected porosity that may not be visible to the naked eye.

The inspection process generally involves several essential stages:

1. Pre-Cleaning
2. Penetrant Application
3. Excess Penetrant Removal
4. Developer Application
5. Inspection and Evaluation

When properly performed, Penetrant Testing provides a practical and effective method for identifying surface-breaking defects in welds, castings, forgings, and various industrial components.

Over the past few months I've been building VenHub (Vendor Hub), an operations portal for vendors and internal teams at iForte Solusi Infotek. Field surveys and FTTH preventive maintenance used to run through many manual steps across several systems. VenHub moves that flow into one portal connected directly to Salesforce.

What VenHub does today: 
1. Connectivity Survey Salesforce sends surveys to vendors. Vendors fill in the Survey Form section by section, with photos per group. After submission, Salesforce creates or updates the Work Report and sends the status (Submitted, Approved or Rejected) back to VenHub.
2. Automatic PHS documents When a survey is Approved, the system calculates quantities against the PHS price list, generates the PDF, and uploads it to the Work Report in Salesforce. Failed deliveries retry automatically and can also be resent manually.
3. FTTH Preventive Maintenance Technicians submit a Customer ID, a category, and evidence photos. The photo count is validated against the category. Salesforce then sends the Work Order and Service Appointment status back.

What's next We plan to move more of the FTTH business process into VenHub, so vendors and internal teams work from one place.

Security and personal data protection VenHub holds customer and vendor data, so I built this in from the start, using Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP) as the reference:
1. Email OTP login, plus mandatory Microsoft Authenticator for Super Admins and Admins
2. Temporary account lock after repeated failed logins, and automatic logout when idle
3. Personal data masked in logs and in views for roles that shouldn't see it
4. Access to personal data recorded: who, which role, which endpoint
5. Automatic data retention for logs, histories and notifications

Tech stack:
1. Backend: Go (Gin), PostgreSQL, JWT, TOTP
2. Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, Zustand, React Hook Form + Zod, acting as a BFF so the browser never handles the API token
3. Integrations: Salesforce (Apex/LWC and REST), internal email service
4. Deployment: Docker & Jenkins

What I learned:
1. Two-way integration needs retries, idempotency, and clear logs, or small failures are hard to trace.
2. Security and privacy cost far less when built in from the beginning.
3. As developers, we have to solve problems, keep learning, and adapt to whatever comes up. We shouldn't idolize a single platform, because a developer needs to see the big picture and pick the tools that will actually help the company.

Thanks to the team who helped along the way Andrey Sholinka, Dwiky Kurniawan, Daffa Asyqar Ahmad Khalisheka, Karina Virgi, Viriya Putta, Jessica Jetje Joanna.

To mark Indonesia Building Day (Hari Bangunan Indonesia, or HBI) 2026, PT Indocement Tunggal Prakarsa Tbk. (Indocement), through its Semen Tiga Roda brand, held four seminars that brought together students, academics, industry professionals and government representatives. The series began with three university seminars in Yogyakarta, Bandung and Jakarta, and culminated in the Indonesia Building Day National Seminar on 11 November 2026 at Pendopo Sapta Taruna in Jakarta.

The university series opened at Universitas Islam Indonesia in Yogyakarta on 31 October 2026. Speakers discussed material selection, efficient resource use and safety during construction. Two further seminars took place on 4 November. At Universitas Katolik Parahyangan in Bandung, the discussion focused on the role of architects in selecting materials and designing buildings that remain energy-efficient throughout their service life. At Universitas Mercu Buana in Jakarta, civil engineering students learnt how sustainability principles are applied in the cement and precast concrete industries and explored Indonesia’s green construction policies.

Following the three university seminars, Indocement and the Ministry of Public Works co-hosted the national seminar under the theme Working Together to Advance Sustainable Construction and Put It into Practice. Hundreds attended in person and online, including representatives from government, construction material manufacturers, contractors, developers and universities.

Indocement President Director Christian Kartawijaya opened the seminar by emphasising the importance of delivering economic and social benefits while taking responsibility for the environmental impact of development. Indro Pantja Pramodo, Acting Director General of Construction Development at the Ministry of Public Works, then delivered the keynote address. Representatives from several organisations marked Indonesia Building Day by sounding a siren, followed by a joint declaration in which all participants took part.

During a panel moderated by the Global Building Performance Network (GBPN), speakers discussed sustainable construction policies, how sustainability principles are being applied to the Giant Sea Wall project, and developments in construction materials and technology. Indocement Director Troy D. Soputro shared examples from the company’s operations, including its use of alternative fuels and solar power. The event concluded with a discussion and Q&A on the challenges of putting sustainable construction into practice in Indonesia.

Indocement hopes the collaboration fostered through the 2026 Indonesia Building Day seminar series will continue and help more projects across Indonesia adopt low-carbon construction practices and use resources more efficiently.

Around the world, governments and property developers have spent billions of dollars building new cities. Modern buildings, smart technology, wide roads, and impressive infrastructure are often presented as signs of progress. Yet, some of these ambitious projects have struggled to attract residents, create jobs, and sustain economic activities.

Why does this happen?

The experiences of Masdar City in the United Arab Emirates, Forest City in Malaysia, Meikarta and Sofifi in Indonesia offer important lessons. Although each project faces different challenges, they highlight a common risk: physical development moving faster than actual economic and social needs.

A city cannot survive simply because its buildings are completed. People need jobs, affordable housing, schools, healthcare, public transportation, and reliable public services. Without these basic needs being met, even the most impressive development can become an expensive and underused asset.

Another common mistake is treating new city development primarily as a property investment opportunity. Selling land and apartments may generate short-term revenue, but it does not necessarily create a sustainable local economy.

Smart technology is also not a guarantee of success. Technology should help solve real problems, rather than become an expensive feature that adds little value to people's daily lives.

As Indonesia considers developing more new cities, we must learn from these experiences. Economic opportunities should be established before large-scale housing construction begins. Legal certainty, institutional responsibilities, infrastructure financing, and consumer protection must be addressed early.

Development should also take place gradually. Each expansion phase should depend on measurable results, such as actual population growth, housing occupancy, job creation, and the financial ability to maintain public infrastructure.

When these targets are not achieved, decision-makers must have the courage to pause, review, and adjust their plans.

Functional beverages are entering a more specific phase of innovation. 

Consumer interest is moving beyond general energy boosts towards more targeted benefits, from focus and mood support to sustained energy throughout the day.

One development worth watching is Zynamite®, a mango leaf extract being studied as a non-stimulant ingredient for cognitive performance. Its potential applications point to an interesting opportunity for F&B brands: exploring functional propositions that don't rely entirely on caffeine.

For product developers, this opens up new formulation possibilities. A beverage designed around focus or cognitive support could appeal to consumers looking for alternatives to conventional energy drinks, or simply a different way to support their daily routines.

But the commercial opportunity depends on a few practical questions. 
Is this benefit relevant to a clearly defined consumer group? 
Does the ingredient work within a formulation that delivers on taste, texture, and stability? 
And can the final product justify its price point while communicating its benefits credibly?

Clinical research can make an ingredient interesting. 
Building a product around it requires a much deeper understanding of consumer needs, formulation constraints, and the market it intends to serve.

The real opportunity lies in translating ingredient innovation into a product that earns a place in consumers' everyday habits.

*Role of Chemical Engineer in Geothermal Industry*

One of the most meaningful aspects of our work is the opportunity to pass on what we have learned to the next generation.

Last Friday, 20 November 2026, I had the pleasure of meeting Chemical Engineering students at the Faculty of Engineering, Universitas Indonesia, Depok, to share perspectives on the role of chemical engineers in the geothermal industry.

Rather than focusing solely on chemical treatment, we explored a broader engineering philosophy: follow the fluid. Understand how changes in the process affect thermodynamics, heat transfer, phase behavior and fluid composition, and connect chemistry with engineering decisions. From reservoir to reinjection, every change in pressure, temperature, phase and composition has implications for power generation, operational reliability, safety and environmental performance.

This is why I believe chemical engineers have a much bigger role to play in Indonesia's geothermal development. Geothermal is not simply about drilling wells or generating steam and electricity. It involves the complex interaction of thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, heat and mass transfer, water and steam chemistry, materials science, corrosion, scaling, process optimization and environmental management. Chemical engineers are uniquely equipped to connect these disciplines and translate fundamental science into practical solutions that make geothermal operations safer, more reliable, efficient and sustainable.

Preparing the next generation for this opportunity also requires an important contribution from academic institutions. Strong engineering fundamentals remain essential, but students must also understand how these fundamentals interact in real industrial systems. Closer collaboration between universities and industry, through real-world case studies, field exposure, internships, applied research and regular engagement with industry practitioners, can help bridge the gap between knowing the theory and solving real-world problems.
This is also part of what Ecolab and Nalco Water can contribute to Indonesia: not just technology and expertise, but also knowledge sharing and capacity building for the next generation of engineers.

Indonesia is blessed with tremendous geothermal resources. But resources alone do not create progress; it is people who turn potential into reality. Hopefully, more young Indonesian engineers will be inspired to strengthen their fundamentals, gain hands-on experience, challenge conventional approaches and apply their knowledge to develop the industries and resources of their own country.

THE RISE OF THE SOLOPRENEUR: SUSTAINABLE BUSINESS MODEL OR GROWTH CEILING?

Singapore's solopreneur economy is growing.

Government data shows 89,800 solopreneurs in 2024, up 55% from 57,800 in 2014. They now represent 25% of resident-owned enterprises.

Around 3,100 generated at least S$1 million in annual revenue without employing anyone.
Impressive. But is this model sustainable when the ambition shifts from earning locally to expanding regionally?

1. REVENUE IS NOT BUSINESS HEALTH
Around 66% generated less than S$100,000 annually. Only 3.4% reached S$1 million. Revenue is not profit. We must also consider costs, cash flow, customer concentration and the founder's actual take-home income.

2. AI ENABLES LEANER OPERATIONS - NOT LIMITLESS GROWTH
AI and automation allow one person to manage work that once required several specialists. But technology cannot replace accountability, customer relationships, quality control or sound decision-making. Efficiency increases capacity. It does not automatically create a scalable business.

3. REGIONAL EXPANSION CHANGES EVERYTHING
Expanding across Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means navigating different consumer behaviours, languages, regulations, payment systems and distribution networks. A business that succeeds through the founder's personal network in Singapore may not replicate that advantage elsewhere. Local partnerships and market knowledge become essential.

4. THE FOUNDER CAN BECOME THE BOTTLENECK
When sales, strategy, delivery, finance and customer relationships depend on one person, growth eventually competes with capacity. What happens when demand doubles or multiple regional clients need attention simultaneously? Without reliable partners, documented processes and delegated execution, complexity can grow faster than profitability.

5. REGIONAL SCALE REQUIRES A DIFFERENT MODEL
The answer is not necessarily a large workforce. A lean core supported by specialist contractors, local partners, technology and clear operating processes may be more sustainable. The objective should be to scale capability and recurring revenue - not simply workload.

MY TAKEAWAY - Solopreneurship is a legitimate business model. Remaining small can be a deliberate and financially sound choice. But regional growth changes the equation.

Having worked more than 02 decade across APAC markets, I know expansion is not simply selling the same proposition in more countries. It requires local execution, partner alignment and operational discipline.

THE REAL TEST IS NOT HOW MUCH ONE PERSON CAN EARN, BUT HOW MUCH THE BUSINESS CAN GROW WITHOUT DEPENDING ENTIRELY ON THAT PERSON.

Have a team in Indonesia, or planning to hire there? 🇮🇩

There is an employment law update worth understanding.

Indonesia’s Employment Protection Law took effect on 28 October 2026. It covers how businesses hire people, manage employment and end working relationships. 

For overseas business owners, this means reviewing both your employment contracts and the costs of managing your Indonesian team.

Hiring someone on a fixed-term contract? These contracts are called PKWT in Indonesia. They have duration limits, prohibit probation and carry compensation obligations.

Extending or ending a contract? An extension can trigger a payment for the completed term. Ending a contract early can create additional costs.

Using an outsourced company? Check which activities can legally be outsourced and who is responsible for the workers. 

Reviewing leave or planning a dismissal? Local entitlements and procedures need to be built into your HR policies.

The law also introduces a severance reserve fund to help ensure employees receive qualifying entitlements when employment ends.

It’s detailed implementation was still being prepared, according to the Manpower Minister’s statement on 17 November 2026. 

Save this post and share it with whoever is managing your Indonesian team. 

Adapted from NAWASENA Law’s November 2026 brief, the legislation and the ministerial update reported by ANTARA.

Please seek Indonesian legal advice for your circumstances.

Across Africa, much of the housing, schools, clinics and workplaces we will need by 2050 is yet to be built. That gives us a rare chance to get them right, and getting them right means the people who use these spaces every day must have a say in how they are designed, built and run.

Women across our continent carry much of the care for families in homes that are often hot, poorly ventilated and costly to run. Yet women are still too few in the rooms where building codes are written, projects are financed and construction sites are managed.

While co-developing Kenya's National Buildings and Construction Decarbonization Roadmap (2026–2040) with the State Department for Public Works Kennedy Matheka and our partners, we saw this clearly. The growing areas of opportunity, such as retrofitting and green materials, still have very few women in them. Gaps in training, hiring, site culture and safety build up over the course of a woman's career. And without deliberate action, the move to low-carbon buildings could deepen the very inequalities we hope to close.

That is why I am so proud of what we have built together. Our JEDI Integration Toolkit, helps bring justice, equity, diversity and inclusion into decarbonisation planning.  Through She Builds Sustainably, we are working with WIRE Kenya, the National Construction Authority and our wider network to grow market-relevant green skills, support women-led businesses and open doors through mentorship and employment partnerships.

Africa's young and fast-growing cities give us the chance to build inclusion in from the start.

posts.text:
Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia's CEO. The company he returned to no longer ships Hopper chips to China.

Last week I asked whether Washington let a scandal become leverage. This time I'm sticking to what's on the record.

Here is what happened in 11 days:

Nov 12: Nvidia announces Huang's resignation. He had admitted an affair amid reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO.

Nov 16: The Commerce Department issues a rule requiring licenses for advanced chips sent to any data center, anywhere, that supplies significant compute to Chinese-headquartered companies. Shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil now need licenses too. The same day, Trump says he "would not mind" seeing Huang back.

Nov 17: On the earnings call, the board chair says the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Kress says Nvidia has stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center chips, including the H200, to China. That was $2.4 billion last quarter, about 2% of revenue. She doesn't say why. The board also forms a committee to oversee national security and export controls.

Nov 23: The board unanimously reinstates Huang. Its statement says it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and, based on that input, is confident his return poses no national security risk. Nvidia is also hiring a new Chief Compliance Officer.

Six days separate "does not intend to" and "unanimously reinstated." The filing names one input in between.

To be clear about what this does not prove: it doesn't prove anyone planned it. The espionage allegations remain unproven. The board's investigation is still open. Huang faces closed-door questions from three House committees on Dec 1 and 2. Beijing had also already restricted H200 imports, so the halt was partly a formality.

Here is what it does show. Huang once called US export policy toward China "a failure." The H200 arrangement with China was brokered between him and the White House. He left on Nov 12. When he returned on Nov 23, those China shipments had stopped, a national security committee sat on his board, and the US government had weighed in on whether he came back.

The founder survived. For now, the China strategy he championed did not.

If you build outside the US on rented GPUs, this matters to you. Compute is now regulated like strategic infrastructure, down to which data center serves which customer. If your stack runs on capacity in Singapore or Malaysia, read the Nov 16 rule now, before your provider sends you a compliance notice.

Who should have the final say over the world's compute layer: founders, boards or governments?

posts.text:
Laziness is not why people stop walking.

That was the first thing our team got wrong in Challenge 2 at Apple Developer Academy @ UC, Jakarta.

Our first idea was simple. People don't move enough, so build a better step tracker. Bigger numbers, cleaner charts.

Then we talked to users. Nobody said "I'm lazy." They said their weekends just disappeared at home. One of them put it plainly: "I spend my whole weekend playing games."

The steps weren't the problem. A game already had their attention, and walking had nothing to compete with it.

So we built FitChick. Your steps become coins, coins open a gacha, and the gacha dresses up a small yellow chick. You walk because the chick is waiting.

This is also the challenge where Apple's native frameworks stopped being documentation and started being bugs I had to fix. HealthKit for steps. SwiftData for the chick's name. SpriteKit for the blinking and wing flaps. A Live Activity for the daily mission.

One month, a team of 5, around 8,800 lines of Swift.

The chick is cute. The real win was learning to ask "why" one more time than feels polite.

If you've built a health app: what turned out to be the real reason your users stopped?

I had never built a screen in SwiftUI. Two weeks later, our team of 6 demoed an 8-screen app.

That was Challenge 1 at Apple Developer Academy @ UC, Jakarta.

The app is called Laras. You pick your communication style (passive, passive-aggressive or aggressive), get matched with partners for a 90-second video discussion, then rate how each other communicated. Every avatar is a cat. Please don't ask why.

How the two weeks actually went:

Ideation first. Sticky notes, long debates, and a lot of "wait, who is this for?"

Then Swift fundamentals. Structs, @State, NavigationLink, and learning why my view refused to update.

Then building. Around 1,600 lines of SwiftUI later, the screens finally talked to each other.

The code is messy. The cats are cute. I'm keeping both.

What surprised me most: the hardest part wasn't Swift. It was disagreeing with 5 people for hours and still liking them at the end.

To mark Indonesia Building Day (Hari Bangunan Indonesia, or HBI) 2026, PT Indocement Tunggal Prakarsa Tbk. (Indocement), through its Semen Tiga Roda brand, held four seminars that brought together students, academics, industry professionals and government representatives. The series began with three university seminars in Yogyakarta, Bandung and Jakarta, and culminated in the Indonesia Building Day National Seminar on 11 November 2026 at Pendopo Sapta Taruna in Jakarta.

The university series opened at Universitas Islam Indonesia in Yogyakarta on 31 October 2026. Speakers discussed material selection, efficient resource use and safety during construction. Two further seminars took place on 4 November. At Universitas Katolik Parahyangan in Bandung, the discussion focused on the role of architects in selecting materials and designing buildings that remain energy-efficient throughout their service life. At Universitas Mercu Buana in Jakarta, civil engineering students learnt how sustainability principles are applied in the cement and precast concrete industries and explored Indonesia’s green construction policies.

Following the three university seminars, Indocement and the Ministry of Public Works co-hosted the national seminar under the theme Working Together to Advance Sustainable Construction and Put It into Practice. Hundreds attended in person and online, including representatives from government, construction material manufacturers, contractors, developers and universities.

Indocement President Director Christian Kartawijaya opened the seminar by emphasising the importance of delivering economic and social benefits while taking responsibility for the environmental impact of development. Indro Pantja Pramodo, Acting Director General of Construction Development at the Ministry of Public Works, then delivered the keynote address. Representatives from several organisations marked Indonesia Building Day by sounding a siren, followed by a joint declaration in which all participants took part.

During a panel moderated by the Global Building Performance Network (GBPN), speakers discussed sustainable construction policies, how sustainability principles are being applied to the Giant Sea Wall project, and developments in construction materials and technology. Indocement Director Troy D. Soputro shared examples from the company’s operations, including its use of alternative fuels and solar power. The event concluded with a discussion and Q&A on the challenges of putting sustainable construction into practice in Indonesia.

Indocement hopes the collaboration fostered through the 2026 Indonesia Building Day seminar series will continue and help more projects across Indonesia adopt low-carbon construction practices and use resources more efficiently.
